..
Issued at 1249 PM CDT Tue Sep 8 2026

Showers continue across northeast Nebraska into west-central Iowa 
this morning. A cool front is slowly pushing south into our area 
which will provide forcing for thunderstorm development this 
afternoon. The environment will be ready. The 850mb jet
continues to bring in a stream of moisture from the Gulf. PWAT 
this afternoon will start around record territory for this time 
of year (1.8-1.9in) and only go up over 2 inches as we see 
moisture pooling along the front advancing south into the 
evening and overnight. Moisture and daytime heating will only 
enhance environmental instability with generally around 
2000-2500 J/kg of SB- and MLCAPE along the surface front. As far
as shear, the more deep-layer shear will be well behind the 
front, but we do see enhancement of the low-level shear (0-1km 
bulk shear and helicity) around 7pm as we see winds increase on 
the nose of the LLJ. 

We're predicting two bands of storms to develop this evening, the 
first will initiate along the surface front around 05-06PM. There is 
some uncertainty in where this band will exactly set up, but 
somewhere along or just south of I-80, southeast into Saline county 
seems likely. The second band will set up north of the surface front 
along a corridor from Boone and Platte Counties through Thurston, 
Burt, and Monona. Storms should initially struggle to 
strengthen with weaker environmental shear. As we see shear 
increase around and after 7PM, there will be a window along the 
southern line where we could see enough low-level shear for a 
tornado or two before this line weakens and the northern line 
becomes more dominant. Once the northern line takes over, expect
more typical elevated thunderstorm threats, mainly being 
damaging winds and large hail.

We are also very concerned with how much rain these storms will 
produce, especially as we go into the overnight hours. With PWATs 
above climatological record territory for this time of year, these 
storms will be VERY efficient rain producers. Going into the 
overnight hours, we see the frontal boundary stall west to east 
across our area with signals indicating likely training of storms 
north of this boundary (the northern line mentioned above). Hi-res 
ensemble guidance indicate a west-east band of 2-4 inches of rain 
likely to set up somewhere across our area anywhere from Norfolk to 
Lincoln. Flash flooding will be a concern for this area overnight 
with the band of rain dropping south around 7am and clearing later 
Wednesday morning. 

Once storms wrap up Wednesday morning, the forecast becomes quieter 
for a couple days as a surface high out of Canada shifts south 
over our area brining in pleasant, seasonable temperatures for 
this time of year. Highs Wednesday and Thursday will only be 
warming into the upper 70s to low 80s across our area with dew 
points dropping into the upper 50s to near 60 Thursday 
afternoon. The upper-level pattern shows the stubborn ridge that
has been keeping our temperatures Hot will be pushed off to the
east and northwesterly flow will be reinforcing the CAA into 
the Central Plains behind the front. 

A more zonal flow regime sets up for the second half of this week as 
ridging over the Desert Southwest fights against an active series of 
troughs moving into the PacNW out of the Gulf of Alaska. The first 
stronger of these troughs will bring a cold front into the Northern 
Plains, leading to an increase in southerly flow across the Missouri 
River Valley late Thursday into Friday. With this we'll see 
temperature warm back up on Friday with highs up into the upper 80s 
to low 90s. Could be breezy in northeast Nebraska closer to the 
front where gusts 35 to 40 mph will be possible. The cold front 
advances south across our area Friday night into early Saturday 
bringing our next chance for thunderstorms, potentially severe. SPC 
has us highlighted under a 15% outlook for Day 4 which usually lines 
up with at least a coming slight or enhanced risk. What may help our 
situation is that we'll be a bit south of the main wave and surface 
low, with the greater potential more likely to our north over 
eastern SD into central MN. Certainly a time period to monitor.

The forecast details get fuzzier over the weekend with another 
strong through over the Inter-Mountain West putting us into more
of a southwesterly flow regime with shortwaves bringing a 
series of chances for showers and storms through the weekend 
into early next week. While it likely won't be continuous rain 
through the period, uncertainty in timing of these waves keeps 
precip chances throughout the rest of the forecast period. 
Temperatures will be cooler with highs mostly in the 70s peaking
around 80 south through the weekend into early next week.
